newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria moves closer to currency board system.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria moves closer to currency board system.

text.p: Bulgaria moved a step closer to launching a currency board system aimed at stabilising its shattered economy on Tuesday after reaching an agreement with the International Monetary Fund on this year's draft budget deficit.
Finance Minister Muravei Radev also announced on Tuesday the reformist government's plans to peg the lev to the mark as an anchor in the currency board at a rate of 1,000 levs.

Under the currency board system, designed to restore confidence in Bulgaria's currency and shaky banks, the lev is fixed to the mark and levs in circulation must fully covered by foreign exchange reserves.

The draft budget unveiled by Radev includes a deficit equal to 6.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), higher than the 3.8 percent recommended by the IMF, partly due to interest payments on foreign and domestic debt.

"The budget deficit is higher than we anticipated because of two main factors: revenues are weaker than we expected due to the stagnating economy and due to recently adopted adjustments for inflation in the personal income tax law," IMF team leader Anne McGuirk told a news conference.
"On the expenditure side interest payments are higher than projected," she added.

Interest payments comprise 9.8 percent of GDP, of which 2.9 percent is envisaged for foreign debt interest payments and 6.9 percent on domestic debt interest, Radev told the same news conference. GDP is estimated at 16.15 trillion levs ($9.8 billion).

"The important question is not the size of the deficit but how it will be financed. It will be financed without any funding from the central bank. Budget funding should come from foreign financing and privatisation," said McGuirk.
Up to 3.4 of the 6.2 percent deficit would be funded by proceeds from privatisation, said Radev. External financing was seen at 1.5 percent and non-bank funding at 1.6 percent.
The draft budget, which has yet to be approved by the cabinet and by parliament, envisages expenditures at 33.5 percent of GDP and revenue at 27.3 percent of GDP, said Radev.
Annual inflation is projected at 566 percent this year. Monthly inflation for May is seen around zero, compared with 243 percent in February amid political and economic instability.
Central bank foreign exchange reserves stood at $1.28 billion in May, up from $1.146 billion in April, governor Lyubomir Filipov said.

Once preparations for the currency board are completed for a July 1 launch, the IMF is expected to disburse a second $130 million tranche of a $510 million stand-by arrangement sealed in April. A third $86 million tranche is earmarked for end-August if Bulgaria meets reform targets.
IMF lending is also linked to Bulgaria's progress in dealing with loss-making companies slated for closure.
Bulgaria's parliament is expected to pass on Wednesday or Thursday amendments to the central bank law. This would reorganise the central bank and appoint a new board.
An article in the central bank law will also stipulate the lev's peg to the mark at a fixed rate of 1,000.
Parliament also needs to revise a banking law to make the currency board operational and finalise this year's budget by the end of June.

Central bank lending to the government in commercial banks is banned. A special banking department will be empowered to provide limited lending only if the whole banking system is threatened. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-981-4145 ($ = 1645 Bulgarian Levs)
